The equation is $\dfrac{1+t}{1-t}=1+4t$, i.e. $1+t=(1+4t)(1-t)=1+3t-4t^2$, i.e. $4t^2-2t=0$, so $t=0$ or $t=\frac12$ (neither is $\pm1$).
As $x$ runs over $(-2\pi,2\pi)$, $\frac x2$ runs over $(-\pi,\pi)$, an interval of length $2\pi$, on which $\tan\frac x2$ takes every real value twice except where $\frac x2=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
$t=0$: $\frac x2\in\{0\}$ only ($\pm\pi$ are excluded by the open interval), so $x=0$, with $\sin x+\cos x=0+1=1$.

$t=\frac12$: $\frac x2=\alpha$ or $\alpha-\pi$, where $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac12$; so $x=2\alpha$ or $2\alpha-2\pi$. For both, $\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}=\frac45$, $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}=\frac35$, so $\sin x+\cos x=\frac75$. Check: $\sec x+\tan x=\frac53+\frac43=3=1+4\cdot\frac12$.
originality_note: New: sec x + tan x written through t = tan(x/2) collapses to (1+t)/(1-t), so the equation becomes a quadratic in t; the root t = 0 survives only at x = 0 because the interval (-2pi, 2pi) is open, and t = 1/2 gives two values of x (way 5). Closest known: the identity sec x + tan x = tan(pi/4 + x/2) and 'sec x + tan x = k' exercises. Different because: the right side also contains tan(x/2), and the answer depends on counting the members of each family in an open interval of length 4pi.

concept_use.Miscellaneous trigonometric equations: The non-standard mixture of sec x, tan x and tan(x/2) is reduced through the simplification sec x + tan x = (1+t)/(1-t).
concept_use.Half-angle substitution t = tan(x/2): sin x = 2t/(1+t^2), cos x = (1-t^2)/(1+t^2) turn the equation into 2t(2t - 1) = 0 and give sin x + cos x for each root.
